Your password is the starting point. A passkey makes signing in quicker and safer, and two-factor authentication adds a second lock. All of it lives in Settings, and none of it involves anyone outside your server. These settings need a connection to your server. While you're offline they're shown read-only.

A passkey lets you sign in with your fingerprint, face or device PIN instead of typing a password. It can't be phished or reused on another site, and your password keeps working as a fallback. Open Settings → Security and find the Passkeys card. Select Add passkey and give it a name you'll recognise, like "Work laptop". Confirm with your fingerprint, face or PIN when your device asks. Next time, choose Sign in with a passkey on the sign-in screen, or pick it from the suggestions in the email field. Add a passkey on a second device too, so losing one isn't a problem. You can rename or delete passkeys in the same list. If one is marked as suspicious, OpenTodo noticed something that looks like a copied passkey; delete it if you don't recognise the device. If you don't see the Security section, passkeys aren't available on your server. They need a secure https:// address; ask whoever runs your server.

With two-factor authentication, signing in takes your password plus a six-digit code from an authenticator app on your phone. Any app that supports time-based codes works. Open Settings → Security → Two-factor authentication and select Set up two-factor authentication. Scan the QR code with your authenticator app, or type in the key shown under it. Enter the six-digit code the app shows. Save the recovery codes that appear. They're shown only once: download them as a text file or write them down and keep them somewhere safe. From then on, sign-in asks for a code after your password. Signing in with a passkey skips the code, because the passkey already checks it's you.

When you enter a code, you can tick Remember this device for 30 days so that browser doesn't ask again for a month. The list of remembered browsers is under Two-factor authentication, where you can forget them.

Each recovery code works once, in place of a code from the app. Use one if you lose your phone. Settings shows how many you have left and lets you generate a new set, which replaces the old one. If you lose both your phone and your recovery codes, the owner of your server can reset your two-factor authentication. Your server's owner can also make two-factor authentication required. If so, you'll be asked to set it up when you sign in, and you can't turn it off.

Open Settings → Security, select Change password in the Password card, enter your current password and a new one of at least 10 characters. Changing it signs you out everywhere else; the device you're on stays signed in. Forgot it? There's no self-service reset by email. Ask the owner or an admin of your server for a reset link. If you're the owner, see recovering owner access.

Settings → Activity → Recent activity lists sign-ins and token changes on your account from the last 90 days. If you see one you don't recognise, change your password, revoke your API tokens and tell the owner of your server.

Some changes, like creating an API token or turning off two-factor authentication, ask for your password or a code again, unless you entered one in the last ten minutes. That keeps someone who finds your unlocked laptop from changing them.
Settings → Account → Session → Sign out ends your session on that device and removes your tasks from it. Changes that haven't been sent yet are uploaded first when you're online.

End-to-end encryption encrypts your task titles, notes and comments on your devices, so even your server only stores scrambled text. If your server uses a company or family login (single sign-on), you can link it under Settings → Security → Linked accounts and sign in with it.
Your tasks are yours. You can download all of them at any time, and bring tasks in from other places. Nothing is locked in.

Open Settings → Data and select Download export (JSON) in the Export row. You get one file with all your projects, sections, tasks and subtasks, labels, reminders and saved views, including completed tasks and items in the Trash. Shared projects you're a member of are included too. The file is plain JSON, so you can open it in any text editor, keep it as a backup, or load it into another OpenTodo server. The person who runs your server can also set up automatic backups of the whole server.

Open Settings → Data, select Import data… (or press g then Shift+I) and choose a file. OpenTodo accepts: an OpenTodo export, for moving to another server or restoring, a CSV file, from a spreadsheet or a script, with a title column and optional columns for project, due date, priority, labels and more, JSON exports from other task apps, in the common shapes those apps use. Nothing is written straight away. OpenTodo first shows a preview: Check the format it detected. You can change it if it guessed wrong. Choose the options: which project gets tasks that have none, the time zone for dates, whether sections stay sections or become labels, and what to do with possible duplicates and with rows that have errors. Read the preview table. Each row says what will happen: created, updated, skipped (with the reason) or an error (with the reason). Problems are listed first. Import. The import runs on the server, and the tasks reach all your devices on their next sync. Recurring rules, reminders, subtasks, sections and completed tasks come across where the file has them. Anything OpenTodo can't store is listed as a warning on its row, never dropped silently.

Importing the same file twice won't double your tasks. OpenTodo recognises rows it imported before, and flags tasks that look like ones you already have (same title, project and due date). Those are skipped unless you choose Import them anyway. For an OpenTodo export, items that already exist on the server are kept as they are, unless you choose to overwrite changed fields.

Every import appears under Past imports, with a summary. Undo removes everything that import created and leaves the rest alone. Tasks you added later to an imported project move to your Inbox rather than disappearing. You can then import the same file again, for example with different options.

Import needs a connection to your server. Files can be up to 20 MB and 50,000 rows, unless your server allows more. Comments aren't imported. The preview tells you how many there were. In a CSV file, write dates as 2026-10-15 and put a time like 09:30 in a due_time column. The import reference lists every column, with an example file. If a JSON export from another app isn't recognised, convert it to CSV. Every field OpenTodo stores can be written as a CSV column. The import formats reference has the details: each format, how fields are mapped, recurring rules and reminders.
Deleting something in OpenTodo doesn't make it vanish. It goes to the Trash first, and every change to a task is kept in its history, so a slip of the finger is easy to undo.

Open Trash in the sidebar (or press g x). It lists deleted tasks and projects, newest first, with when they were deleted and how many days they have left. Select Restore next to an item. It comes back exactly where it was: A restored project returns to its place in the sidebar, with all its tasks. A restored task returns to its project. If that project is still in the Trash, the task goes to your Inbox instead. With the keyboard: j / k to select, r to restore.

Delete permanently removes one item for good, and Empty Trash removes everything in it. Both ask you to confirm, and both need a connection. Once something is permanently deleted, it's gone from every device and from the server, and it can't come back. Items are also deleted for good automatically after 30 days in the Trash. Your server's owner can change that period or turn it off.

Deleting a task also deletes its subtasks. Deleting a project hides it and its tasks everywhere. Its sub-projects move up a level, so they aren't lost. Reminders on deleted tasks stay quiet. Restore the task and they work again. Deleted items are still in your export until they are deleted for good.
See what changed on a task

Open a task and select the History tab below its details. Changes are grouped into versions, newest first: everything one person changed from one device within a few minutes is one version, with a one-line summary such as "Renamed and rescheduled", who made it, where (this device, another device, the API, a calendar app, or an AI assistant) and when. Select a version to see each change: the old value struck through and the new one next to it, shown the way the task shows them (dates in your date format, priorities, labels, project and section names). A change marked not applied arrived after a newer one and never took effect; you can still restore it. Changes made by an AI assistant read "AI assistant (token name)" for your own assistants and "AI assistant" for someone else's in a shared project, and can be restored like any other change. Projects have a History too, at the top of the project. History is loaded from your server, so it needs a connection. Offline, the tab says so instead of showing anything out of date.

Next to each change in a version is Restore this value. Select it to set the field back to that value. To put back everything a version changed at once, select Restore this version; a confirmation lists the fields first. Restoring is a change like any other: it syncs to all devices and shows up in the history itself as a new version, so you can always undo the undo. Each field is restored as its own change, so if someone edits the same field on another device at the same time, the later edit wins for that field.

The Activity tab of a task shows who created it, completed it, moved it or changed the date, newest first. Quick changes by one person within ten minutes are grouped into one line, such as "You changed the due date and priority"; select it to see each change. Comments appear as one short line that opens the comment. Activity works offline; your changes that are not synced yet are marked pending. In shared projects this includes everyone's changes. See Sharing and comments.

Archiving is different from deleting. An archived project disappears from the sidebar, but it isn't in the Trash and isn't deleted after 30 days: it and its tasks are kept as they are. Archive a project from its Project menu. When you complete the last task of a project, OpenTodo offers to archive it. Projects without open tasks for 30 days are archived automatically, with a notice that has an undo button. To switch automatic archiving off on a device, untick the option under Settings → Projects.

Open Settings → Projects. Under Archived projects you see every archived project, with its parent project and how many open tasks it has. Select Restore next to one, and it's back in the sidebar with all its tasks. With the keyboard, Tab to the button and press Enter. Restoring works offline, like any change, and the project comes back on your other devices after they sync. Restoring brings back that one project. If you archived a project with sub-projects, they stay in the list until you restore each of them. A project you restore by hand isn't archived automatically again on that device. In a shared project, only the owner or an admin can restore it, the same people who can archive it.

Open Settings with the gear next to your name at the bottom of the sidebar, or press g then s. Settings opens on your profile card (your initials, name, email and role) and the sections, grouped under You, App, Data and connections and, for the people who run the server, Server. Each section has an icon and a line saying what's inside. Pick one to open it. On a wide screen the grouped list of sections stays on the left while you work in one, and the current section is highlighted. On a phone, each section starts with a ← Settings link back to the list. Every section has its own address, such as /settings/integrations, so you can bookmark it or share a link with someone on the same server. Older links keep working: /settings/general opens Preferences. Inside a section, each panel is a card. It leads with its current state (for example whether two-factor authentication is on and how many recovery codes are left), then its settings as rows with the control on the right. Forms with several fields open from a button, and actions that remove something ask you to confirm first and say what will be lost. Some settings follow your account to every device. Others belong to the device you're on, so your phone and laptop can be set up differently. Settings that apply to one device say "this device" next to them. Each panel has a Help link on the right that opens its part of this guide next to Settings. What you see depends on your role: the owner and admins also see the Server group, and
Your profile card and Sign out of this device. Signing out removes your tasks from this device; changes not yet sent are uploaded first, and the app asks you to confirm.

Password: Change password opens the form. See Account security. Two-factor authentication: a code from your phone on top of your password. The card shows whether it's on and how many recovery codes are left, and warns when only a few remain. See Account security. Passkeys: sign in with your fingerprint, face or device PIN. See Account security. Linked accounts: connect a single sign-on login, if your server offers one.
Encrypt your task text on your devices, and keep its recovery key. See End-to-end encryption.
Sign-ins and token changes from the last 90 days. The owner also sees the server's Audit log here.

How the app behaves on this device. Appearance: light or dark, and a colour theme, on all your devices (see below). Start view: the view this device opens on. See Views. Date and time: how dates and times look and where weeks start, on all your devices (see below). Calendar: when the Day and Week grid starts and ends, and how long your working day is. See Time blocking. Keyboard: turn on Vim keybindings. See Keyboard shortcuts. Appearance Mode: System follows your device's light or dark setting (the default), Light and Dark keep the app that way whatever the device says. Each tile previews its theme; with the keyboard, the arrow keys move between them. Both apply at once, without a reload, and follow your account to every device, also when you change them offline. They never change other people's app. Priority colours (P1 to P4), warnings and errors, and the colours of your projects, labels and views keep their meaning in every theme. The installed app's title bar follows the theme too; the splash screen when it starts stays neutral, because it is the same for everyone on the server. Every theme meets the same contrast rules in light and dark. Push notifications for reminders on this device, and a test that shows whether they arrive. See Notifications.

Quick add: turn natural-language parsing on or off, pick the languages it understands, and the order of day and month in dates like 12/11. See Quick add syntax. Voice capture: dictate tasks into quick add. Off until you turn it on, and the app explains first what your browser does with the audio. See Quick add syntax. Bookmarklet and extension: the Add to OpenTodo bookmarklet, to save the page you're reading as a task. See Capturing pages. Email to task: your own secret address; emails sent there become tasks. See Email to task.
Archive projects automatically after 30 days without open tasks, and bring back archived projects with Restore. See Trash and history.
Download export (JSON) saves everything you have in one file. Import data… brings in tasks from a file. See Import and export. The sync status of this device is shown too.

These panels connect OpenTodo to other tools. Some appear only when the person running your server has switched the feature on. Calendar apps (CalDAV): see your tasks in calendar and reminder apps on your phone or computer, with an app password. See Calendar apps. Webhooks: send a message to another service when tasks change. See Webhooks. API tokens: keys for scripts and the ot command-line client. A token is shown once, when you create it. Read-only tokens can't change anything; tokens for an AI assistant that can make changes work only through the assistant tools and never on the rest of the API. See HTTP API and Command-line client.

Assistant: the in-app assistant, when the server owner has turned it on: your consent, which assistant you use (the server's, or your own Anthropic, OpenAI or Gemini provider, model and key, if allowed), this month's usage, Apply small changes without review (this device) and Clear conversations on this device. The owner also chooses the provider, models, keys, network and monthly allowance here. See AI assistant. AI assistants: give an AI assistant read-only access to your tasks, or, when the server owner allows it and you switch on Allow AI assistants to make changes, a token for an assistant that can make changes you can undo. See AI assistants (MCP). A token you create here is also listed under Integrations → API tokens.
Only the owner and admins see this group; Backups and Access policies are for the owner only.

Users: everyone with an account, their role and last sign-in. Make someone an admin (owner only), deactivate or reactivate an account, create a password reset link, or delete an account. Members: invite people with a single-use link. See Sharing and comments.

Scheduled backups to a folder, S3 or WebDAV, the last run and its result, and the next one. Restore from a backup puts the whole server back to an archive from the destination or one you upload: you see a verified preview first, type RESTORE to confirm, and the server restarts into the restored data. Undo last restore puts the previous database back, and old safety copies can be deleted to free space. See Backups.

Two-factor policy: optional, required for the owner, or required for everyone. See Account security. Single sign-on: sign-in through your company or family identity provider. See Single sign-on. Project invite links: Members can invite new people with project links (off by default) lets links that members create in a project's Share dialog also create accounts. See Who can bring new people. Running the server itself is covered in Running with Docker.
Most problems have a quick fix. Start with the section that matches what you see. If nothing here helps, the person who runs your server can look at its logs, or you can open an issue on GitHub.
A task seems to be missing

Check these places, in this order: A filter above the list. If Quick wins, Under 30 min, Over 1 h or Unestimated is switched on, the list shows only matching tasks. Select it again to clear it. Completed. It may have been ticked off by accident. Open Completed and reopen it. Trash. It may have been deleted, or its project was. See Trash and history. An archived project. Tasks of archived projects don't appear in Today or Upcoming. A folded parent or section. Select the small arrow to unfold it. A shared project you left or were removed from. Ask its owner. The Filter view with search: word (add & completed to include finished tasks) searches titles and notes.
Changes don't show up on my other device

Look at the status at the top right of both devices. Offline · 3 pending means the changes are still waiting on that device; they're sent as soon as it's online. Click the status to sync right away. Sync error: hover over it to see the reason. If the server is down or being updated, it clears up once the server is back. Signed out: your session ended. Sign in again; waiting changes are sent afterwards. Locked: your account uses encryption. Enter your passphrase on that device. See Offline and sync for what each status means.

Check the email address and that Caps Lock is off. Passwords are at least 10 characters. After several failed attempts, the server makes you wait a little before trying again. Forgot your password? OpenTodo doesn't send reset emails. Ask the owner or an admin of your server for a reset link. If you are the owner, see recovering owner access. Lost your two-factor phone? Use one of your recovery codes instead of the code. Without them, the server owner can reset your two-factor authentication.
The demo says my sandbox expired
Demo sandboxes are deleted after two hours without activity, after 24 hours at most, and every night. Select Start a new sandbox to get a fresh one. Nothing from the old sandbox is kept.

Inside the app, reminders pop up while it's open. To get them when the app is closed, push notifications must be turned on for each device in Settings → Notifications, and on an iPhone only the installed app can receive them. Notifications lists the messages you might see and what to do.
I can't install the app or add a passkey

Both need your server to be on a secure https:// address. If the browser offers no install option, or Settings has no Security section for passkeys, ask whoever runs your server. Instructions per device are in Installing the app.

If a word was read as a date, project or priority by mistake, select the × on its chip before you press Enter, or press Backspace twice at the end of the line. Text in double quotes is never interpreted: Read "Next Friday". You can also switch parsing off in Settings → Capture → Quick add. See Quick add syntax.
I can't edit a shared project
Your role in that project is viewer, which is read-only. Ask the owner or an admin to make you an editor. See Sharing and comments.
I can't share a project with someone
You can only add people who have an account on your server. Ask an admin of the server to invite them first. Accounts with end-to-end encryption turned on can't share new projects.
The app looks out of date
The app updates itself when your server is updated. If something still looks old, close it completely (all tabs or the installed window) and open it again.
If a part of the app fails to display, you see a message with a Reload button. Your tasks are stored on the device and aren't lost by reloading.
Yes. Each device keeps a full copy of your tasks, and changes are sent when you're back online. See Offline and sync.
On your devices and on the OpenTodo server you use. Nothing goes to anyone else: the app has no tracking and no analytics, and it only talks to your own server.
Is there an app in the app stores?
No. OpenTodo is a web app that you install from your server's address, and it then behaves like any other app. See Installing the app.
Can I use OpenTodo on my own, without a server?

OpenTodo needs a server to sign in and sync, but it can be small: a single container on a Raspberry Pi or a cheap virtual server is enough. To try it first, use the demo. Setting up a server is described in Running with Docker.
Can I move my tasks from another task app?
Usually, yes. OpenTodo imports CSV files and the JSON exports of other task apps. See Import and export.
Can several people use one server?
Yes. The owner invites people, each person has their own account and private tasks, and projects can be shared between them. See Sharing and comments.

Type one line in the quick-add box (press q in any task view) and OpenTodo picks out the due date and time, project, labels, priority and estimate: Meeting with Sarah next Wed at 3pm #work @call p1 +30m creates Meeting with Sarah, due next Wednesday at 15:00, in project Work, with the label call, priority 1, estimated at 30 minutes. Everything runs in your browser. The parser needs no network, sends nothing anywhere, and gives the same result on every device for the same line, date, languages and projects. The created task stores the resolved date, so other devices never parse the line again.

Before voice capture can be switched on, Settings shows this statement and waits for you to confirm: Speech is recognised by your browser, not by OpenTodo. Depending on the browser, your audio may be sent to the browser vendor's speech service (for example Google for Chrome, Apple for Safari) and handled under their privacy policy. OpenTodo asks the browser to recognise speech on this device when it offers that choice. Your OpenTodo server never receives audio or transcripts. Only the task you save with Enter is stored and synced, like a typed one. The microphone is used only while you dictate; the browser asks for permission the first time. OpenTodo's code never records, stores or sends audio: the Web Speech API hands it text. On-device recognition is requested whenever the browser reports it available for the language (Chromium's processLocally); OpenTodo never asks the browser to download a speech model. The browser asks for microphone permission on your first dictation, not when you switch the setting on.

Recurrence ("every Monday") and reminders ("remind me at 9") are set in the task's detail panel (see recurrence.md and reminders.md), not in the quick-add line. ! (not) binds tightest, then & (and), then | (or). @errand | @call & p1 means @errand | (@call & p1). Use parentheses to group: (@errand | @call) & p1. & and | are the only connectives. There is no implicit "and": @work p1 is an error, write @work & p1. Whitespace between tokens is ignored, so due<=tomorrow and due <= tomorrow are the same.

A bare name (@errand, #Work) runs until whitespace, a double quote, or one of the operator characters & | ! ( ) < > =. Any other character, including #, -, /, . and non-Latin letters, is part of the name. Put names with spaces or operator characters in double quotes: #"Client A", @"follow up". Inside quotes, \" is a literal quote and \\ a literal backslash. Keywords, comparison words, weekday names, label names and project names all ignore case: #work, #Work and #WORK are the same.

A task can repeat. The rule is a short English phrase stored in the task's recurrence field, for example every weekday or every 3 days after completion. The same grammar is implemented by the server (internal/recurrence) and the web app (web/src/lib/recurrence.ts), and both are tested against one shared file of test vectors (web/src/lib/recurrence.vectors.json), so every device and the REST API compute the same dates. Every example on this page is one of those vectors.

every <pattern> [after completion] [until YYYY-MM-DD | for N times] Rules are case-insensitive and extra whitespace is ignored. A rule is at most 200 characters. What gets stored is the canonical form: lowercase, single spaces, weekday names spelled out, ordinals with the correct suffix. Every 2nd Tuesday is stored as every 2nd tuesday. Pattern Examples Meaning day, N days every day, every 3 days Daily, or every N days (1–999). week, N weeks every week, every 2 weeks Every 7 × N days. weekday every weekday Monday to Friday. month, N months every month, every 6 months Same day of month; a day the month does not have becomes its last day. year, N years every year, every 2 years Same date; 29 February becomes 28 February in common years. weekday names every monday, every mon, wed, fri, every tuesday and thursday Any set of weekdays, full names or three-letter abbreviations, separated by commas or "and". day of month every 1st, every 15th, every 31st That day of each month; in shorter months the last day. last day every last day The last day of each month. last weekday every last weekday The last Monday–Friday of each month. ordinal weekday every 2nd tuesday, every first monday, every last friday 1st/first to 4th/fourth or last of that weekday in each month. every 2nd is the 2nd day of each month; every 2nd tuesday is the second Tuesday.

Add after completion to a day, week, month or year interval to count from the day the task is actually completed instead of from its due date: every 3 days after completion, every week after completion. Calendar patterns (weekdays, days of month, ordinals) cannot be completion-relative.

until YYYY-MM-DD: no occurrence after that date, e.g. every day until 2026-12-31. for N times: the series has N occurrences in total, e.g. every weekday for 10 times. Skipped occurrences do not count. Only one end condition per rule.
How the next occurrence is computed

All dates are floating calendar dates (YYYY-MM-DD), like due itself; the computation never converts through a time zone, so daylight saving changes have no effect. The due time, if any, is kept. Calendar rules: the next occurrence is the first matching date strictly after the current due date. If that date is already in the past (the task was overdue), it is instead the first matching date after today: overdue tasks catch up rather than piling up, and no missed occurrences are generated. Interval rules keep their rhythm while catching up (every 3 days due on the 1st, completed on the 10th, moves to the 13th). Completion-relative rules: the next occurrence is counted from the local date of completion. every 3 days after completion due Monday and completed on Wednesday is next due Saturday; completed on the Sunday before, it is next due Wednesday. Month ends: every month due 31 January moves to 28 (or 29) February. The rule has no memory of the original day, so the following month is the 28th too; use every 31st or every last day to stay at the end of the month. A rule set on a task without a due date gives it one: the first matching date from today on.

Complete: a completed copy of the current occurrence (the occurrence record) goes to Completed, and the task moves to its next occurrence. When the end condition is reached the task completes like any other task. Skip (Shift+S, or Skip in the detail panel): moves the task to the next occurrence without recording a completion. Completion-relative rules skip as if completed today. Skipping the last occurrence is not possible; complete or delete it. This occurrence only (Shift+O, or the button in the detail panel): makes a standalone copy of the current occurrence, without a rule, and moves the series to its next occurrence. Edit or move the copy freely. Every other edit (title, notes, project, priority, labels, due time, rule) applies to the series, because the series is the task. Reopen an occurrence record and it becomes a standalone open task; the series is not moved back. Reopening a series that ended keeps its rule, so its next completion continues the schedule.

The rule is stored in task.recurrence and occurrence records point back with task.series_id (see sync.md). An occurrence record's id is derived from the series id and the occurrence date (SHA-256, formatted as a UUID), and the next due date is a pure function of the rule and dates every device shares. Two devices that complete the same occurrence offline therefore write the same record and the same next due date, and end with one Completed entry once they sync. A for N times count is the number of occurrence records, so it converges without a counter. The REST API behaves the same: PATCH /api/v1/tasks/{id} with a non-null completed_at on a recurring task records the occurrence and moves the task (see api.md). Clients older than this feature keep working: they store the new fields without showing them and complete a recurring task as a plain completion, which is recovered by reopening it on an updated device.

A task can carry any number of reminders (OpenSpec change reminders). Open a task, then use the Reminders section of the detail panel. Relative reminders fire a number of minutes before or after the task's due time ("30 minutes before"). A task with a date but no time counts as due at 09:00. A task whose time is fixed to a time zone fires relative to that exact instant, wherever your devices are. When the due date or time changes, on any device or through the API, the reminder moves with it; recurring tasks carry their relative reminders to the next occurrence. Without a due date a relative reminder is kept but does not fire. Absolute reminders fire at a moment you pick and never move with the due date. They work on undated tasks and are shown in each device's local time.

Reminders are personal. On a task in a shared project your reminders are yours alone: other members never see or receive them, and you can add them with any role, viewer included. When someone else moves the task, your relative reminders follow as soon as one of your devices syncs.

In the app. While the app is open, a reminder whose time has come appears as a notification in the corner with Snooze 10 min, 1 hour, Tomorrow 09:00 and Dismiss (focus moves to it; Esc dismisses). This needs no network and no permission, and is skipped for completed or deleted tasks. When the tab is in the background and the browser allows notifications, a system notification is shown instead. Web push. In Settings → Notifications each device can enable push so reminders arrive while the app is closed. Enabling asks for the browser permission and registers the device with the server; disabling or signing out removes it. The server checks for due reminders every 30 seconds and sends each one once per firing time to every enabled device of the reminder's owner (reminders are personal), then records the delivery on the reminder (an op by device server) so all devices know it fired. System notifications offer Snooze 10 min and Dismiss; these work offline and are uploaded on the next sync. If the app is focused when a push arrives, the reminder is shown in the app only. Privacy. A push payload carries only the reminder id, the task id and the firing time, encrypted end to end (RFC 8291) so the push service cannot read it. The device shows the title from its own copy of the task. Enable Include task titles if a device should be able to show the title before it has synced the task; the description is never sent.

A reminder does not fire, in the app or by push, while its task is deleted or while the task's project, or any project above it, is in the Trash. It is not marked as delivered either, so restoring the task or the project brings it back: a reminder whose time is still ahead fires on time, and one whose time passed while it was in the Trash is delivered once, late, on the next check (the same rule as for reminders that fell due while the server was down). Dismiss or snooze it if you no longer need it. Purging the task from the Trash removes its reminders.

Snoozing sets a new firing time (in 10 minutes, in an hour, or tomorrow at 09:00) and the reminder fires again, also by push. Dismissing silences the current firing. Both are ordinary synced edits: when one device dismisses and another later snoozes the same reminder, the later edit wins on every device.

For an account with end-to-end encryption the server never puts a title in a push, even for devices that opted in to titles: it cannot read it, and ciphertext would be useless. The notification uses the content-free text; in-app reminder toasts still show the decrypted title from the device.

Nothing to configure. The VAPID key pair is generated on first use at <data>/push_vapid.pem and travels with backup archives. OPENTODO_PUSH=off turns push off entirely (routes answer 404, no outbound requests); in-app reminders keep working. Push requires the app to be served over https (OPENTODO_BASE_URL), as browsers only allow push subscriptions on secure origins. See self-hosting and API.

The title is cut to 500 characters, the text to 16 KB with a [truncated] note. A link is kept only if it starts with http:// or https://; anything else (javascript:, data:, file: …) is dropped and the rest of the share is shown normally. Shared content is shown as plain text, never as HTML, and the capture screen never opens the shared link. There is no auto-save: a link to /share cannot create a task without you pressing Save. Files and images cannot be shared yet; the app is offered in the share menu for text and links only.

OpenTodo imports tasks, projects, sections, recurrence rules and reminders from files: its own JSON export (for moving between instances or recovering), CSV from a spreadsheet or a script, and the JSON exports of other task managers. Open Settings → Data → Import data in the web app (or press g then Shift+I), or drive the same endpoints from a script; see API below. Every import works in two steps: Preview. The server reads the file and reports, row by row, what would happen: create, update, skip (with a reason) or error (with the row number and the reason), with totals that also count new sections, recurring tasks and reminders, and file-level notes (for example comments that are not imported). Nothing is written. Import. The server runs the import as a background job. Every created or changed field becomes an ordinary operation in the op log, stamped with server time and the device id import, so every device receives the imported data on its next sync under the usual last-writer-wins rules. A whole import can be undone later. Import runs on the server, so it needs a connection: the Import screen disables the file picker while offline and keeps showing the last loaded job list.

The format is detected from the content, in this order; the preview shows what was detected and the format option overrides it. An archive with more than 1,000 files, mixed formats, an unsafe file name, or more than ten times the upload limit when unpacked is refused with 400 invalid_file before anything is written. A zipped Things Database.thingsdata

The file from Settings → Data → Download export or GET /api/v1/export. Labels, projects (with their sub-project tree), sections, tasks (with subtasks, completion and tombstones), reminders and saved views are recreated with their original ids and field values, so importing an export into an empty account and exporting again gives an equivalent file (comments aside, see below). Because ids are kept, nothing needs remapping: a task's section_id, a recurring series and its occurrence records (series_id, whose ids are derived from the series id), a reminder's task_id and a dashboard's panels all point at the same entities as before. Every task field is carried: recurrence (stored in canonical form, for example Every Monday becomes every monday), series_id, section_id, notes_doc (rich-text notes), due including a zoned tz, estimate_minutes and ical_extra. What is handled differently, and why: Comments are not imported. A comment keeps its author, and the sync engine only accepts comments whose author_id is the account writing them; the authors in an export are accounts of the exporting instance (and other members of shared projects). Comment creation is also rate-limited per account. Rewriting every comment to you would misattribute other people's words, so the preview shows a note such as "12 comments are not imported" and nothing is written for them. On a Mac, open ~/Library/Group Containers/JLMPQHK86H.com.culturedcode.ThingsMac/, then the ThingsData-… folder, and copy Things Database.thingsdatabase. Upload its main.sqlite (right-click the folder and choose Show Package Contents), or a ZIP of the whole folder. On iPhone or iPad the article describes a diagnostics code that sends Things Database.aar; tap it to unpack it into the same folder. The file is read from a private copy on the server, read-only, using only Things' own tables, and deleted after the preview or import. A SQLite file that is not a Things database is refused with 400 invalid_file. UTF-8, with a header row. Comma, semicolon and tab separators are detected from the header; quote fields that contain the separator. Header names are case-insensitive and spaces or dashes count as underscores (Due Date is due_date). Only title is required. A top-level array of task objects, or an object with a tasks array and an optional projects array ({id, name, parent_id}; parent_id makes sub-projects). Key names are matched leniently: Task attribute Keys read title title, name, content, summary, text description description, notes, note, body project project_id (an id from projects), or project / project_name / list (a name) section section, section_name, column, heading parent parent_id, parent, or nesting under subtasks / children priority priority: 1–4, p1–p4, high/medium/low/none due due, due_date, dueDate, deadline: a string, or {date, time?} / {datetime} labels labels, tags: strings, {name} objects or a comma-separated string completion completed, done, checked (booleans), status: "completed", and completed_at / completedAt for the time created created_at, createdAt, created recurrence recurrence, rrule, repeat, recurring, recurrence_rule, recurrenceRule, repeatRule, or a due object with is_recurring and its string; a string, an array of RRULE strings or a {frequency, interval, days} object reminders reminders, reminder, alarms, reminder_at, remind_at, reminderDateTime: one value or an array

An object with projects, sections, items and optionally labels, notes and reminders arrays joined by ids. Source Becomes projects[].name, parent_id project and sub-project; the source inbox (inbox_project: true) maps to the target project items[].content, description title, description items[].project_id, section_id project, section sections[] sections of their project, created even when empty, in file order (with sections: section; deleted ones are skipped) items[].parent_id subtask items[].priority counted upwards in the source: 4 → 1, 3 → 2, 2 → 3, 1 → 4 items[].due.date due date (date-times with a zone are converted) items[].due.is_recurring, due.string recurrence rule from the due string (every tue 4pm → every tuesday, every! 2 weeks → every 2 weeks after completion); a string that cannot be expressed is a warning reminders[] (item_id) type: "relative" with minute_offset → reminder that many minutes before the due time; type: "absolute" with due.date → reminder at that time; location reminders and is_deleted ones are dropped (location with a warning) items[].labels label names items[].checked, completed_at, added_at completion, completion time, creation time notes[], deadline, duration dropped with a warning on the item Items and projects marked is_deleted are skipped.

{"lists": [{"id", "title", "tasks": [...]}]}; each list becomes a project with its title. Tasks read title, notes (description), due (RFC 3339; converted to the chosen time zone), status: "completed" and completed (completion time), parent (a task id) or nested subtasks, and starred / important (priority 1). recurrence (string, RRULE array or {pattern: {type, interval, daysOfWeek}}) becomes a rule and reminderDateTime (or the other reminder keys of json-generic) a reminder. links are dropped with a warning; tasks marked deleted are skipped.

Projects are matched by name, ignoring case, against existing non-deleted projects; otherwise created. Tasks without a project go to the target project (option) or the Inbox. Sections: see Sections. Recurrence and reminders: see Recurrence and Reminders. Subtasks are resolved after the whole file is read, so row order does not matter. A subtask joins its parent's project. A parent that is missing, invalid or would form a cycle leaves the task at the top level with a warning. Labels are matched by name, ignoring case; missing ones are created. Dates: plain dates stay dates; date-times without a zone keep their wall clock; date-times with a zone become the wall clock of that instant in the chosen time zone (default: the browser's zone in the web app, UTC through the API). Due dates are always stored floating. Completion: a completed row keeps its source completion time, or the import time when the source has none. Unsupported attributes (attachments, comments, assignees, links, location reminders, recurrence rules the grammar cannot express) never block a row: the task is imported and the row carries a warning naming what was dropped.

With sections: section (the default) a row's section becomes a real section of the task's project: an existing live section with the same name (ignoring case) is reused, otherwise one is created once per project, after the existing ones. A subtask's section is looked up in the project it ends up in. Tasks without a project (the Inbox, when no target project is chosen) cannot hold sections, so their section becomes a label, with a warning. sections: label turns every section into a label named like it (the behaviour before sections existed), sections: ignore drops them. Re-importing a file finds the sections it created by name (and, for json-items, by source id), so nothing is duplicated.

A recurrence becomes a rule of the recurrence grammar, stored in canonical form, when the grammar can express it. Accepted, in this order: The grammar itself: every day, every 2 weeks, every monday, friday, every 15th, every last friday, every 3 days after completion, … until 2027-01-01, … for 10 times. An iCalendar RRULE, with or without the RRULE: prefix (FREQ=WEEKLY;INTERVAL=2, FREQ=MONTHLY;BYDAY=-1FR), when it maps exactly onto a rule (as for CalDAV). Common spellings: daily, weekly, monthly, yearly, annually, biweekly, fortnightly, every other day|week|month|year, weekdays, every workday, every weekend, each … and ev … for every …, and every! … for "after completion" (every! 3 days → every 3 days after completion). A trailing time of day (every tue 4pm, every day at 09:00) is removed: the due time carries it. A structured object {frequency|freq|type|unit, interval, days|daysOfWeek|byday} (also under pattern), e.g. {"frequency": "weekly", "days": ["MO", "TH"]} → every monday, thursday, and an array of RRULE strings. Anything else (hourly rules, starting …, every other monday, an interval combined with weekdays, free text) is shown in the preview as a warning on the row, recurrence "every 3 hours" not supported; imported without a rule, and the task is imported without a rule. A recurring task without a due date gets the rule's first date from today in the chosen time zone, as in the app. Imported recurring tasks are series of their own (no series_id).

Reminders are created together with their task (a task that is skipped, for example as already imported, brings none) and belong to you, like every reminder. Value Becomes a number, or a string of digits relative reminder that many minutes before the due time 30m, 1h, 2 days, 15 min before relative reminder before the due time an ISO 8601 duration (-PT15M, -P1D) relative reminder; a negative duration is before the due time a date-time (2026-10-20T08:00, with or without zone) or a date absolute reminder at that time (floating values in the chosen time zone, a date at 09:00) an object with offset_minutes (negative = before), minute_offset / minutes_before (minutes before) or offset / trigger (a duration) relative reminder an object with datetime, at, remind_at, fire_at, time, date or due.date absolute reminder type: "location" dropped with a warning A relative reminder fires at the due time plus its offset, with a date-only due counting as 09:00, in the chosen time zone. On a task without a due date it is kept but does not fire (the row says so). A reminder whose time has already passed at import time is imported dismissed, with a warning, so no stale notification is sent. Offsets beyond one year are dropped with a warning.

Checked in this order: Own export: an id that already exists is skip (exists) or, with existing: overwrite, update. A source row recorded by an earlier, not undone import of the same format for this account is skip (already_imported). Importing the same file twice therefore creates nothing the second time. CSV rows without an id column are recognised by their content. A row whose title (trimmed, ignoring case), project and due date match an existing open task is skip (possible_duplicate), unless the duplicates option is import, in which case it is created with a warning.

Option Values Default format a format id from the table above detected targetProject id of one of your projects Inbox timeZone IANA zone, e.g. Europe/Rome UTC (the web app sends the browser zone) sections section, label, ignore section duplicates skip, import skip errors skip_rows, abort skip_rows existing skip, overwrite (own export only) skip With skip_rows, bad rows are reported and everything else is imported; a bad row never leaves a partial task. With abort, any row in error fails the job before anything is written and names the first bad row.

One import job per account runs at a time; starting a second one answers 409 conflict naming the running job. Files may be at most OPENTODO_IMPORT_MAX_MB megabytes (default 20, allowed 1–200) and 50,000 rows; larger files answer 413 too_large. Ops are written in batches of at most 1,000 and progress is saved after each batch. If the server restarts mid-import, the job shows failed with the counts of what was written, and undo removes it. Undo tombstones every project, task, label, section, reminder and saved view the job created, through the op log: they disappear from every view and from other devices after their next sync, and stay in the export with deleted_at. Entities the job only updated are left alone. As when deleting in the app, open tasks you later added to an undone project move to the Inbox, open tasks you later put into an undone section move to "No section", and undone labels are removed from your other tasks. Undo is idempotent. After an undo the same file can be imported again. Webhooks see an import as one import.completed delivery per finished job and one import.undone per undo, not one event per task. See Webhooks → Imports. Job records (status, options, counts, row errors) are operational metadata kept in the server database; they are not part of the export.

The preview reads the whole file once. CSV is streamed record by record; a JSON file is decoded in one piece and takes roughly five times its size in memory, so the largest default file (20 MB of JSON) peaks around 100–120 MB during the preview and the start of the job, released afterwards. Typical imports of a few thousand rows stay under 10 MB. On a 1 GB Raspberry Pi keep the default or lower OPENTODO_IMPORT_MAX_MB.

All routes require a session or a bearer token, like the rest of the API. Uploads are multipart/form-data with a file part and the options either as one JSON options part or as individual fields named like the options. # Preview (nothing is written) curl -sS "$OT/api/v1/import/preview" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -F file=@tasks.csv -F timeZone=Europe/Rome # Start the job → 202 {"job": {"id": "…", "status": "running", …}} curl -sS "$OT/api/v1/import" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -F file=@opentodo-export.json -F 'options={"existing":"overwrite"}' # Follow it, list jobs, undo curl -sS "$OT/api/v1/import/jobs/<id>" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" curl -sS "$OT/api/v1/import/jobs" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" curl -sS -X POST "$OT/api/v1/import/jobs/<id>/undo" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" See docs/api.md for the response shapes and error codes.

Optional, per account, off by default (OpenSpec change e2ee). When it is on, your devices encrypt the content of your tasks before it is synced, so the server, its backups and every server-side integration hold only ciphertext for it. Sync, offline use and conflict-free merging keep working because ciphertext travels through the unchanged operation log as an ordinary string value. Turn it on in Settings → Encryption.
What is encrypted, what is not

Encrypted, in your personal data (Inbox, your own projects, labels, saved views): Entity Encrypted fields task title, description, ical_extra, notes_doc (the rich-text note document, encrypted as one opaque string; its ciphertext must fit the 256 KB document limit, so an encrypted note document is capped at about 196 KB) project name label name section name saved view name, query comment body (your comments on your own tasks) Everything else stays plaintext, because views sort and group by it, reminders and calendars schedule with it, and the server needs it to merge and authorize: due (date, time, zone), priority, completed_at, deleted_at, created_at, position, project_id, parent_id, section_id, labels (the list of label ids on a task), recurrence, estimate_minutes, assignee_id, project color and archived, reminder times, and all timestamps and device ids of operations. Empty values ("") and null are not encrypted. The length of a ciphertext reveals the approximate length of the text. Shared projects are never encrypted. A project that was shared before you enabled encryption, and projects other people share with you, stay plaintext for every member. While encryption is on you cannot share a project that is not shared yet (409 encryption_enabled): the members would hold no key.

Protected against: Someone who reads the server's disk, database file, backups (local, S3, WebDAV) or database dumps: they see ciphertext for the fields above. The server operator browsing the data, and server-side integrations (CalDAV, the MCP endpoint, webhooks, the REST API with an API token): they see ciphertext or a placeholder. A server or a bug moving a ciphertext to another field or task: the value is bound to entity, entityId and field and fails authentication; the app shows "[Cannot decrypt]" and keeps the operation. Not protected against (honest limits): Metadata. Everything in the plaintext list above, plus how many tasks, projects and labels you have, when you edit what, from how many devices, and the approximate length of each text. A malicious or compromised server serving tampered JavaScript. The web app is delivered by the same server it protects you from. A server that changes the code can capture the passphrase or the key on the next load. This is inherent to web-delivered end-to-end encryption; a future change may verify release signatures in the service worker. Your devices. The device is the trust boundary: local storage (IndexedDB) holds plaintext and the account key (as a non-extractable CryptoKey). Malware, a browser extension with access to the page, or someone with your unlocked device can read everything. "Lock this device" forgets the key and pauses sync but leaves already synced data in local storage; Sign out clears local data. Weak passphrases.

Key hierarchy, all generated and used in the browser with the built-in Web Crypto API (no dependency): Account key: 256 random bits, AES-256-GCM. Kept on each unlocked device as a non-extractable key in IndexedDB. Passphrase key: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256 over your passphrase (NFC-normalised) with a 16-byte random salt and 600,000 iterations, producing an AES-KW key. Recovery key: 256 random bits, shown once as 56 base32 characters in 14 groups of four (52 for the key, 4 for a checksum). HKDF-SHA-256 (fixed salt, info opentodo/e2ee/recovery-kek/v1) turns it into an AES-KW key. The account key is wrapped (AES-KW, RFC 3394) under both. The key record — {version, kdf, salt, iterations, wrappedByPassphrase, wrappedByRecovery} — is the only key material the server stores (encryption_keys table). It never receives the passphrase, the recovery key or the account key. Value format (a string in the existing op value): "enc:v1:" + base64url( nonce(12 bytes) || AES-256-GCM(utf8(plaintext)) || tag(16 bytes) ) additional authenticated data = utf8(entity + "\0" + entityId + "\0" + field) Nonces are 96 random bits per encryption. Known-answer vectors shared by the Go and browser test suites are in web/src/lib/e2ee.vectors.json. Where it happens on the device: Every edit is applied locally in plaintext and queued. The sync engine encrypts content fields at the single point where operations leave the device (just before upload), so nothing reaches the server in plaintext whichever path created the

New device: sign in, then enter the passphrase (or the recovery key) on the unlock screen. Nothing is pulled or pushed before that; the sync status reads Locked. Afterwards the device works offline and does not ask again. Wrong passphrase: an error, and after 5 failures within a minute further attempts are delayed for the rest of that minute (on this device). Lock this device (Settings): forgets the key and pauses sync until unlocked. Offline unlock works once the device has seen the key record. A device that did not know encryption had been enabled notices the first ciphertext it receives, checks the key record and locks itself without applying the batch.

Change passphrase (needs the current one and a fresh sign-in confirmation): re-wraps the account key; content is not re-encrypted; other devices keep working; new devices use the new passphrase. Reset with the recovery key (forgotten passphrase): sets a new passphrase and issues a new recovery key; the old one stops working. Lost both: the content cannot be recovered by anyone, including the server owner — there is no server-side reset. Settings and the unlock screen offer only to turn encryption off and delete the encrypted content: the key record is removed and every item whose content cannot be decrypted is moved to the Trash as it syncs. Plaintext fields (dates, structure) are kept.
Enabling, plaintext that appears later, purging, disabling

Enabling re-writes every content field of your personal data as ciphertext through ordinary operations, with progress in Settings; the job is resumable after a reload. 500 tasks produce roughly 1,500 operations. Plaintext written later — through the REST API, the CLI, email-to-task or an import — is accepted by the server and shown with a small "not yet encrypted" marker; the next unlocked device that syncs it re-writes it as ciphertext ("encrypt-on-sight"). Two devices doing that at once produce two ciphertexts of the same text; one wins and nothing is re-written again. Purge plaintext history (POST /api/v1/encryption/purge-history) deletes the superseded operations of the content fields in your personal data, including the plaintext from before encryption. Winners stay, so every device still converges. The deletion runs with SQLite secure_delete, then the database is vacuumed and the write-ahead log truncated. Revision history for those fields is gone afterwards. Backups made before the purge, and copies of the database, may still contain plaintext: delete them if that matters to you. Disabling (needs an unlocked device and a fresh sign-in confirmation) deletes the key record first, so other devices stop encrypting, then re-writes all content as plaintext. Devices that still hold the key decrypt ciphertext that arrives late and re-write it as plaintext too.

The server cannot decrypt. Each feature that needs content degrades explicitly: Feature Behaviour for an encrypted account REST API reads Return the ciphertext string in content fields, plaintext elsewhere. Scripts need the key to decrypt (format above). REST API writes Accepted in plaintext; encrypted on sight by the next unlocked device. Export (GET /api/v1/export) Ciphertext content, plaintext scheduling fields, and the wrapped key record under encryption, enough to decrypt elsewhere with the passphrase. Importing it into another account keeps the ids (so the binding still matches), but that account needs the same key record to decrypt. Import Writes plaintext like REST; duplicate detection by name/title cannot match encrypted labels and projects, so an import may create duplicates. Backups Hold ciphertext and the wrapped key record (plus any plaintext not yet purged). CalDAV Refused: /dav/ answers 403 for the account and creating an app password answers 409 encryption_enabled. Calendar clients can neither read ciphertext nor write it back, and placeholders would overwrite real titles. MCP (assistants) Encrypted titles, descriptions, project, label and section names read as "Encrypted item" with "encrypted": true; search_tasks never matches them. Dates, priorities and structure are still reported. Write tools that need readable text are not offered and are refused with encryption_enabled; scheduling, completing, moving, priorities and labels still work. Email to task Creat
See api.md: GET/PUT/DELETE /api/v1/encryption/keys, POST /api/v1/encryption/purge-history, encryption and minClientVersion in GET /api/v1/me and GET /api/v1/auth/status.

git clone https://github.com/pixari/opentodo.git cd opentodo cp .env.example .env # optional docker compose up -d Open http://localhost:8080. The first visitor creates the owner account. On a server that is reachable from the internet before you open it, set OPENTODO_SETUP_TOKEN (16+ characters) in .env: the setup screen then asks for it, so nobody else can claim the server first. It has no effect once the owner exists. To add more people, keep sign-up closed and create single-use invitation links in Settings → Administration → Members (see Adding people). OPENTODO_ALLOW_SIGNUP=true opens registration to anyone who can reach the server and is rarely what you want on a public URL. Data lives in the named volume opentodo-data, mounted at /data. Change the host port with OPENTODO_PORT in .env. Every variable in the configuration table can be set in .env; the compose file passes them to the container. With docker run, pass them with -e. To build locally instead of pulling: replace image: ghcr.io/pixari/opentodo:latest with build: ..

OpenTodo speaks plain HTTP on 8080 and expects the proxy to terminate TLS. Set OPENTODO_BASE_URL to the public https URL so cookies are marked Secure, the origin check matches and invitation links point at the public address. The server also honours X-Forwarded-Host for the origin check and X-Forwarded-For for rate limiting and the audit log. It trusts only the last X-Forwarded-For hop, the address your proxy appended (Traefik, Caddy, and nginx with proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; append it); earlier entries come from the client and are ignored. So run exactly one proxy in front of the container and do not publish the container port, or a client could send its own header. A CDN in front of your proxy (Cloudflare's orange cloud, or another proxy of yours) adds its own hop, so every visitor would look like the CDN's address and share one rate-limit bucket. Tell OpenTodo which hops to skip with the optional OPENTODO_TRUSTED_PROXIES: a comma-separated list of IP addresses and CIDR prefixes, and the keyword cloudflare for Cloudflare's published edge ranges (built in, no network request). With cloudflare, a request that reaches your proxy from a Cloudflare edge is attributed to its CF-Connecting-IP header, which also works when your proxy drops the incoming X-Forwarded-For. Only set it when every request really comes through those proxies. OPENTODO_TRUSTED_PROXIES=cloudflare Entries may be separated by commas or spaces, and the keyword is case-insensiti

Email to task needs no port, proxy rule or DNS record: OpenTodo makes one outbound IMAP connection (TLS, port 993 by default) to the mailbox you configure with OPENTODO_EMAIL_*. If your host restricts outbound traffic, allow that one host and port. Keep the password in a Docker secret and point OPENTODO_EMAIL_IMAP_PASSWORD_FILE at it (example in the guide).

When the owner enables CalDAV, calendar apps use /dav/ and /.well-known/caldav with WebDAV methods (PROPFIND, REPORT, MKCALENDAR, PROPPATCH). Most proxies (Caddy, Traefik, nginx) forward them unchanged; make sure no rule limits methods to GET/POST or blocks /.well-known/, and that the Authorization header is passed through. App passwords travel in every request, so serve CalDAV over https only.
Passkeys need an https base URL

Passkeys (Settings → Security → Passkeys) are only offered when OPENTODO_BASE_URL is an https:// URL; browsers refuse WebAuthn on plain-http origins. With no base URL or an http:// LAN address, the server keeps working with passwords and simply hides passkeys (auth/status reports passkeysAvailable: false). For local development http://localhost:8080 also works, because browsers treat localhost as secure. Passkeys are bound to the host of that URL (the relying-party id, for example todo.example.com). If you move the server to a new domain, existing passkeys stop matching: users sign in with their password and register new passkeys from Settings. Paths and ports do not matter, only the host. See SECURITY.md for the credential model. Caddy example: todo.example.com { reverse_proxy opentodo:8080 }

Each open tab keeps one long-lived request open, GET /api/v1/sync/events, a server-sent event stream the server uses to tell devices "new changes, sync now". It needs nothing special from Caddy, Traefik (Coolify) or nginx with default settings, because the server already: sends Cache-Control: no-cache and X-Accel-Buffering: no (nginx honours the latter and stops buffering that response), flushes after every write and sends a : ping heartbeat every 25 s, below the usual 30–60 s idle timeouts, caps streams at 16 per account and closes them cleanly on shutdown. Things to keep in mind: Buffering. If a proxy buffers whole responses (older nginx configs with proxy_buffering on and no respect for X-Accel-Buffering, or some CDN "optimisation" layers), the stream never opens. For nginx add proxy_buffering off; to the location that proxies OpenTodo, or at least proxy_http_version 1.1; and leave X-Accel-Buffering enabled. Idle timeouts. Any read/response timeout on the proxy shorter than 25 s will cut the stream (the client reconnects, but it is wasteful). The defaults of Caddy, Traefik and nginx (proxy_read_timeout 60s) are fine. HTTP/2 is recommended. Browsers allow only six HTTP/1.1 connections per origin, and every open tab holds one for the stream. Terminate TLS at the proxy with HTTP/2 (the default for Caddy and Traefik with https) and the streams are multiplexed over one connection. On plain HTTP/1.1 keep the number of open tabs small. Troubleshooting "live updates disconnected"

Reminders are shown in the app on every device and, for devices that enable notifications in Settings → Notifications, sent as web push so a closed app still notifies. Nothing needs configuring: on first use the server generates a VAPID key pair at <data>/push_vapid.pem (mode 0600). Keep it with the database: it is included in backup archives and restored with them, and existing subscriptions only work with the key they were created for. Push is the only outbound traffic that is on by default (webhooks, backups to S3 or WebDAV, single sign-on and email to task contact only what you configure; see Privacy). A push goes to the push service the user's own browser chose when it subscribed (Google, Mozilla, Apple…), carries an encrypted payload the push service cannot read, and by default contains only ids (the device opts in to task titles). Browsers require https for push, so set OPENTODO_BASE_URL to your public https URL (it is also sent as the VAPID contact). To forbid outbound traffic set OPENTODO_PUSH=off: the push routes answer 404, no push is sent, and reminders are still shown in the app.

The MCP endpoint at /mcp is off until the owner enables it in Settings → AI → AI assistants (or OPENTODO_MCP=true presets it on the first start). It is read-only unless the owner also allows assistant changes (OPENTODO_MCP_WRITES=true presets that on the first start) and a user allows them for their account. It needs no extra port or container: assistants reach it through the same URL and reverse proxy as the app, with an API token in the Authorization header. Proxies that buffer or rewrite requests need nothing special, since every answer is a plain JSON response (no event stream). The server makes no outbound request for it. If your proxy logs request headers, exclude Authorization.

The assistant is off until the owner turns it on in Settings → AI → Assistant. There is no environment variable for it: providers, models and keys are set in Settings, and keys are stored in /data/secrets/assistant.json (mode 0600), which backups never include. While it is off, the server makes no request to any model provider. When it is on, the server makes outbound HTTPS requests only to the provider the owner enabled (and, when the owner lets members bring their own key, to the built-in host of the provider a member chose for their key) and only while someone is waiting for an answer (plus Test connection, for the owner and for a member's own provider): Provider Host Anthropic api.anthropic.com OpenAI api.openai.com Google Gemini generativelanguage.googleapis.com Compatible endpoint the base URL the owner entered If your host restricts outbound traffic, allow that one host (or all three built-in hosts when members may use their own provider). Members can never enter a base URL. Requests to the three built-in hosts honour the usual HTTPS_PROXY environment variable. A compatible base URL is checked like a webhook target: it is resolved before every connection, private, loopback, link-local and cloud-metadata addresses are refused unless the owner ticks Allow private endpoints (needed for Ollama or LM Studio on your network), the connection goes to the address that was checked, redirects are never followed, and no proxy is used.
